doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

title: Playing in Europe and black musicians excluded from the symphony
summary: European audiences are intellectuals; he recounts how jazz was despised, white players came later, and black musicians like Coleman Hawkins were shut out of symphonies yet established the saxophone.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Have you played in Europe? Tell us about playing outside the United States. © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -6-

Well in Europe it’s a different ball game. The people in Europe, well almost all the people that come to a jazz festival or jazz clubs are intellectuals or students. And they feel that this is the only art form that American gave to the world was this music. And so they accept us, in fact, there was a time that they felt that nobody white could play jazz, because everybody black was playing it. There was a time that there were very few white guys that even thought of playing jazz. Because like I say it was a lowdown. You know there was one time they called it “whorehouse music” you know. It had every kind of derogatory name that you could think of, and white musicians didn’t want to be associated with that kind of music. It wasn’t until 19 what 1919 or 1918 that with the rhythm, the Original Dixieland Band that came on the scene, and that’s when white guys started playing it. But before then they didn’t play that. Everybody was for the symphony. Everybody was trying for the symphony. blacks too. The only thing, they wasn’t accepted. They couldn’t join the symphony because they said they played it with a jazz feeling. So they wasn’t able to get into the symphony orchestra. So there was a lot guys that learned cello and violin, like Coleman Hawkins was a cello player. But he couldn’t get a job in the symphony orchestra. Well I mean in fact the black musicians are responsible for the saxophones. Because the classical trained musician called it a bastard instrument, because they didn’t use it in the symphony. And they were responsible for the saxophone, I mean being accepted, it was the black musicians, Coleman Hawkins and those kind of people.
